title: The First Phase: The Status Quo in Madinah at the Time of Emigration
arabicTitle: المرحلة الأولى: أحوال المدينة وقت الهجرة

topics.title: A New Society being built

paragraphs.text: Emigration to Madinah could never be attributable to attempts to escape from jeers and oppression only, but it also constituted a sort of cooperation with the aim of erecting the pillars of a new society in a secure place. Hence it was incumbent upon every capable Muslim to contribute to building this new homeland, immunizing it and holding up its prop. As a leader and spiritual guide, there was no doubt the Noble Messenger (Peace be upon him), in whose hands exclusively all affairs would be resolved. In Madinah, the Prophet (Peace be upon him) had to deal with three distinctively different categories of people: his Companions, the noble and Allah-fearing elite; the polytheists still detached from Islam who were purely Madinese tribes; and the Jews.

As for his Companions, the conditions of life in Madinah were totally different from those in Makkah. There they had striven for one corporate target but were scattered, overpowered and forsaken, and their means fell short of establishing a new community; the Makkan Chapters of the Qur'ân were confined to delineating Islamic precepts and enjoining good and forbidding evil. In Madinah, all the affairs of their life rested in their hands — civilization, construction, economics, politics, government, war and peace, worship, ethics. They were at full liberty to erect the pillars of a new Muslim community, distinctive in the world at large. Such a society could not be built overnight; it required time during which legislation ran gradually alongside mind cultivation and education — Allah undertaking legislation and His Prophet (Peace be upon him) implementation: "He it is Who sent among the unlettered ones a Messenger from among themselves, reciting to them His Verses, purifying them, and teaching them the Book and Al-Hikmah." [62:2] And: "And when His Verses are recited unto them, they increase their Faith." [8:2]

The Muslims in Madinah consisted of two parties: the first already settled in their abode, land and wealth, but with deeply-seated seeds of discord and chronic enmity — they were Al-Ansar (the Helpers); the second were Al-Muhajirun (the Emigrants), homeless, jobless and penniless, their number increasing day by day, which strained Madinah's already modest economy, aggravated by the anti-Islamic economic boycott.

The purely Madinese polytheists had no control over the Muslims. Some nursed no grudge and were skeptical of their ancestors' practices, soon embracing Islam sincerely; but others harboured evil intentions yet were too cowardly to resist publicly, faking amicability. 'Abdullah bin Ubai, who had almost been given presidency over Al-Khazraj and Al-Aws after the War of Bu'ath, headed that group of hypocrites; the Prophet's advent foiled his ambitions, so he feigned Islam while disbelief lay rooted in his heart, exploiting events and weak-hearted converts to scheme against the believers.

The Jews (the Hebrews), who had migrated to Al-Hijaz from Syria following Byzantine and Assyrian persecution, assumed the Arabian stamp in dress, language and manner of life, with instances of intermarriage, yet retained their ethnic particularism and prided themselves on their Jewish-Israeli origin, spurning the Arabs as illiterate. They desired their neighbours' wealth to be lawful to them: "...because they say: 'There is no blame on us to betray and take the properties of the illiterates (Arabs).'" [3:75] Religiously they showed no zeal; their commodity was fortune-telling, witchcraft and the secret arts, while they excelled at earning money and trading, monopolizing cereals, dates, wine and clothes, and practising usury — lending the Arab notables great sums and seizing their fertile land as surety. They were very good at corrupting and scheming, sowing discord between adjacent tribes to keep the upper hand and gain interest on loans spent in inter-tribal warfare.

Three famous Jewish tribes constituted the demographic presence in Yathrib: Banu Qainuqua' (allies of Al-Khazraj), Banu An-Nadir, and Banu Quraizah (allies of Al-Aws), who inhabited the suburbs. Naturally they held the new changes with abhorrence, for the Messenger was of a different race, and because Islam came to bring rapport, terminate enmity, and pave the way for an Arab unity that would work to the prejudice of the Jews' social and economic interests. Ibn Ishaq, on the authority of Safiyah (May Allah be pleased with her), narrated that her father Huyayi bin Akhtab and her uncle Abu Yasir went to see the Prophet (Peace be upon him) at Quba' and returned dejected; she heard her uncle ask, "Is it really he?" and her father answer, "It is he, I swear by Allah!" — "Did you really recognize him?" — "Yes, and my heart is burning with enmity towards him."

By contrast, 'Abdullah bin Salam, the most learned rabbi among the Jews, came to the Prophet (Peace be upon him) on his arrival, asked him certain questions to ascertain his Prophethood, and embraced Islam on hearing the answers, but feared his people would slander him. The Prophet (Peace be upon him) sent for some Jews and asked them about 'Abdullah bin Salam; they testified to his scholarly aptitude and virtue — until it was divulged that he had embraced Islam, whereupon they described him as the most evil of all evils. That was the Prophet's first experience with the Jews.

Five hundred kilometres away in Makkah lay another source of threat, the archenemy Quraish. For ten years the Muslims had been subjected to terrorism, boycott, harassment and starvation; on emigrating, their wealth was seized, wives detained, and the humble tortured, while Quraish schemed against the Prophet's life and enticed the Arabs against Madinah. To quote Muhammad Al-Ghazali: "A state of war virtually existed between the Makkan tyrants and the Muslims in their abode. It is foolish to blame the Muslims for the horrible consequences that were bound to ensue in the light of that long-standing feud." The Muslims in Madinah were completely eligible to confiscate the wealth of those tyrants and mete out exemplary punishment to deter them.

The Messenger of Allah (Peace be upon him) arrived in Madinah on Friday, 12th Rabi' Al-Awwal 1 A.H. (27th September 622 A.D.) and took the downstairs of Abu Ayyub's house as a temporary residence. The first task he attended to was the construction of a Mosque, on the very site where his camel had knelt. The land, belonging to two orphans, was purchased; the Prophet (Peace be upon him) himself carried adobe bricks and stones while reciting: "O Allah! no bliss is there but that of the Hereafter; I beseech You to forgive the Emigrants and Helpers." The ground was cleared, the polytheists' graves dug up and levelled, and the Qiblah constructed to face Jerusalem. The Mosque was square, each side about 100 yards; nearby, rooms were built for the Prophet's household, and to the north a place (As-Suffah) reserved for those with neither family nor home. The Adhân was initiated at this early stage. The Mosque was not merely a place of prayer but an Islamic league, an assembly place, and the headquarters from which all the Muslims' affairs were administered.

The Prophet (Peace be upon him) next cemented the ties of mutual brotherhood between Al-Ansar and Al-Muhajirun — unique in the history of the world. A gathering of 90 men, half Emigrants and half Helpers, assembled in the house of Anas bin Malik where the Prophet (Peace be upon him) gave the brotherhood his official blessing; each pair inherited from the other until the verse was revealed at Badr restoring the usual rule: "But kindred by blood are nearer to one another regarding inheritance." [8:75] Sa'd bin Ar-Rabi', a Helper, offered his brother 'Abdur Rahman bin 'Awf half his property and to divorce one of his two wives for him; but 'Abdur Rahman declined, asking only to be directed to the market, where he soon prospered. The Helpers even asked that their orchards be divided with their brethren, but the Prophet (Peace be upon him) instead arranged that the Emigrants work alongside them and share the yield — a wise policy of mutual brotherhood that resolved many problems.

topics.topicSummary: Migration was not mere escape but the building of a new society. In Madinah the Prophet ﷺ faced three groups: his Companions (split into the settled Ansar and the destitute Muhajirun), the Madinese polytheists (some sincere, others hypocrites under 'Abdullah bin Ubai), and the scheming Jews (three tribes who resented the new order). With Quraish still a threat 500 km away, the Prophet ﷺ built the Mosque as the community's heart and forged the unique bond of brotherhood between Ansar and Muhajirun — a policy of selfless sharing that resolved many problems.

topics.title: A Charter of Islamic Alliance

paragraphs.text: Just as the Prophet (Peace be upon him) had established a code of brotherhood amongst the believers, so too he was keen on establishing friendly relations between the Muslims and the non-Muslim tribes of Arabia. He established a sort of treaty aiming at ruling out all pre-Islamic rancour and inter-tribal feuds, meticulous not to leave any area that would allow pre-Islamic traditions to sneak in.

Among its provisions: "This is a document from Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah, concerning Emigrants and Helpers and those who followed and strove with them. They are one nation to the exclusion of other people. The Emigrants of Quraish shall pay blood money among themselves and ransom their prisoners honourably; every tribe of the Helpers likewise. Believers shall not leave anyone destitute among them by not paying his redemption or blood money. Whoever is rebellious or seeks to spread enmity and sedition, the hand of every God-fearing Muslim shall be against him, even if he be his son. A believer shall not kill another believer, nor support a disbeliever against a believer. The protection of Allah is one, extended equally to the humblest of believers. Whosoever of the Jews follows us shall have aid and succour. The peace of the believers is indivisible; no separate peace shall be made when believers are fighting in the way of Allah. Whenever you differ about a matter, it must be referred to Allah and to Muhammad."

It was solely by his wisdom and dexterity that the Prophet (Peace be upon him) erected the pillars of the new society. He used to bring up his followers in the light of Islamic education, sanctify their selves, and infuse into them the ethics of amity, glory, worship, and obedience to Allah and His Messenger. A man asked which merit is superior in Islam; he replied: "That you provide food and extend greetings to one whom you know or do not know." 'Abdullah bin Salam said the first words he heard the Prophet (Peace be upon him) say were: "Extend peace greetings amongst yourselves, provide food to the needy, maintain uterine relations, observe prayer at night while people are asleep, then you will peacefully enter the Garden (Paradise)."

Among the sayings he inculcated: "The Muslim is that one from whose tongue and hand the Muslims are safe." "None amongst you believes (truly) till he likes for his brother that which he loves for himself." "He will not enter Paradise whose neighbour is not secure from his wrongful conduct." "A Muslim is the brother of a Muslim; he neither oppresses him nor fails him. Whosoever removes a worldly grief from a believer, Allah will remove from him one of the griefs of the Day of Judgement." "Abusing a Muslim is an outrage and fighting against him is disbelief." "To remove something harmful from the road is charity." "Charity erases sins just as water extinguishes fire." "He is not a perfect believer who goes to bed full while knowing that his neighbour is hungry." "Show mercy to people on earth so that Allah will have mercy on you in heaven." "Clothing an under-clad Muslim entitles you to a garment from Paradise; feeding a hungry Muslim will make you eligible for the fruit of Paradise; and if you provide water to a thirsty Muslim, Allah will provide you with a drink from 'the Sealed Nectar'."

He also said: "The believers, in their mutual love, are like the human body: when the eye is in agony, the entire body feels the pain; when the head aches, all the body suffers." And: "The bonds of brotherhood between two Muslims are like parts of a house, one part strengthens and holds the other." And: "Do not have malice against a Muslim, nor be envious; do not forsake him. O slaves of Allah, be like brothers. It is not lawful for a Muslim to desert his brother for over three days." 'Abdullah bin Mas'ud said: "Follow the steps of Muhammad's Companions; they were the best in this nation, the most pious, the most learned and the least pretentious. Allah chose them to accompany the Prophet (Peace be upon him) and establish His religion." Those were the attributes on which the Prophet (Peace be upon him) wanted to build the most honourable society ever known in history.

topics.topicSummary: Alongside brotherhood among believers, the Prophet ﷺ drew up a charter binding Emigrants, Helpers and allied tribes into one nation — regulating blood money, mutual defence, protection of the weak, and referral of disputes to Allah and His Messenger. He simultaneously cultivated his followers with a wealth of teachings on greeting, feeding the needy, loving for one's brother what one loves for oneself, good neighbourliness and charity — the moral foundations of the most honourable society in history.

topics.title: A Cooperation and Non-Aggression Pact with the Jews

paragraphs.text: Soon after emigrating and making sure that the pillars of the new Islamic community were well established on strong bases of administrative, political and ideological unity, the Prophet (Peace be upon him) commenced to establish regular and clearly-defined relations with non-Muslims, solely to provide peace, security and prosperity to all and bring about rapport within his region. Geographically, the closest people to Madinah were the Jews. Whilst harbouring evil intentions and bitter grudge, they showed no resistance, and the Prophet decided to ratify a treaty with them granting full freedom in faith and wealth, with no intention of banishment, seizure or hostility.

The most important provisions were: The Jews of Bani 'Awf are one community with the believers; the Jews shall profess their religion and the Muslims theirs. Each shall be responsible for their own expenditure. If attacked by a third party, each shall come to the assistance of the other. Each shall hold counsel with the other, and mutual relations shall be founded on righteousness, sin excluded. The wronged party shall be aided. The Jews shall contribute to the cost of war so long as they fight alongside the believers. Madinah shall remain sacred and inviolable for all that join this treaty. Any disagreement shall be referred to Allah and His Messenger. The signatories shall boycott Quraish commercially and extend them no support. Each shall contribute to defending Madinah against a foreign attack in its respective area. This treaty shall not hinder either party from seeking lawful revenge.

After the ratification of this treaty, Madinah and its suburbs turned into a coalition state, with Madinah proper as capital and Muhammad (Peace be upon him) as 'president'; authority lay mainly in the hands of the Muslims, making it a real capital of Islam. To expand the zone of peace and security, the Prophet (Peace be upon him) started to enter into similar treaties with other tribes living around 'his state'.

topics.topicSummary: Having secured the internal unity of the Muslim community, the Prophet ﷺ made a cooperation and non-aggression pact with the Jews — his nearest neighbours — guaranteeing them freedom of religion and wealth, mutual defence and counsel, the inviolability of Madinah, and a commercial boycott of Quraish, with disputes referred to Allah and His Messenger. This effectively turned Madinah into a coalition state with the Prophet ﷺ at its head.

topics.title: The Prophet on the Battlefield

paragraphs.text: The Quraishites, mortified at the escape of the Prophet (Peace be upon him) and jealous of his growing power in Madinah, kept a stringent watch over the Muslims left behind and persecuted them. They also initiated clandestine contacts with 'Abdullah bin Ubai bin Salul, chief of the Madinese polytheists and president-designate of Aws and Khazraj before the emigration, sending him a strongly-worded ultimatum to fight or expel the Prophet, or else face a military campaign. His pride wounded, 'Abdullah bin Ubai responded positively and mobilized his supporters, but the Prophet (Peace be upon him) summoned and admonished him, and his men gave up the idea; their chief, however, remained a wicked accomplice at heart.

Skirmishes began to pave the way for confrontation. Sa'd bin Mu'adh went to Makkah to observe 'Umrah under the tutelage of Omaiya bin Khalaf; Abu Jahl saw him at the Sacred Sanctuary and threatened to kill him had he not been with Omaiya. Sa'd defiantly challenged him at the risk of cutting off their caravan routes. Quraish then sent the Muslims a note threatening to put them to death in their own homeland; reliable information confirmed real plots, so precautionary measures were taken, including security guards around the Prophet's house. 'Aishah reported that the Prophet (Peace be upon him) once said, 'Were there a pious person from amongst my Companions to keep watch for me tonight,' and then they heard the clang of arms — it was Sa'd bin Abi Waqqas, who said: 'I came to serve as your sentinel.' The Prophet (Peace be upon him) invoked blessings on him and slept.

This close vigilance continued until the Words of Allah were revealed: "Allah will protect you from mankind." [5:67] The Prophet (Peace be upon him) then peeped from the dome of his house and asked his guards to go away, making clear that Allah would protect him. The threats targeted not only his life but the whole entity of the Muslims, and the desert bedouins outlawed them all. At this juncture, Allah gave the Muslims permission to take up arms: "Permission to fight is given to those (believers) who are fighting them, because they have been wronged, and surely Allah is Able to give them victory." [22:39] This came in a larger context of Divine instructions to eradicate falsehood and honour the rites of Allah: "Those (Muslim rulers) who, if We give them power in the land, order for Iqamat-as-Salât, pay the Zakat, enjoin Al-Ma'ruf, and forbid Al-Munkar." [22:41] The permission to fight was revealed in Madinah after emigration, though the exact date is in doubt.

The permission to fight being there, it was wise for the Muslims to bring the commercial routes leading to Makkah under their control. To realize this, the Prophet (Peace be upon him) had two options: entering into non-aggression pacts with the tribes inhabiting the areas adjacent to the routes (he had already signed such pacts with the Jews and other neighbouring tribes), and despatching successive armed missions for harassment along the strategic commercial routes.

topics.topicSummary: Quraish kept persecuting the Muslims left in Makkah and pressured 'Abdullah bin Ubai to fight or expel the Prophet ﷺ, while threatening Madinah directly. After a period of close vigilance — guards like Sa'd bin Abi Waqqas standing sentinel — the verse [5:67] assured the Prophet ﷺ of Allah's protection, and he dismissed the guards. With Quraish bent on aggression, Allah granted the wronged believers permission to fight [22:39], and the Prophet ﷺ moved to secure the Makkan trade routes through pacts and armed missions.

topics.title: Pre-Badr Missions and Invasions

paragraphs.text: The Muslims commenced real military activities, at first in the form of reconnaissance patrols to explore the roads around Madinah and build alliances with nearby tribes. The Prophet wanted to impress upon the polytheists, Jews and bedouins that the Muslims had smashed their old fears and were too strong to be attacked with impunity, and to deter Quraish from military folly against him. The following is a resume of these missions: Saif Al-Bahr Platoon (Ramadan 1 A.H.), led by Hamzah bin 'Abdul Muttalib with 30 Emigrants, to intercept a Quraish caravan of 300 including Abu Jahl; Majdi bin 'Amr prevented a clash. On this occasion the Prophet (Peace be upon him) accredited the first flag in Muslim history — white, carried by Kinaz bin Husain Al-Ghanawi.

In Shawwal 1 A.H., 'Ubaidah bin Al-Harith was sent with 60 horsemen to Batn Rabegh, where they met Abu Sufyan with 200 men; there was arrow-shooting but no fighting, and two Muslims (Al-Miqdad bin 'Amr and 'Utbah bin Ghazwan) defected from Quraish to join 'Ubaidah. In Dhul Qa'dah 1 A.H., Sa'd bin Abi Waqqas was sent with 20 horsemen, instructed not to go beyond Al-Kharrar; they found the Quraish camels had left the day before. In Safar 2 A.H. came the first invasion led by the Prophet (Peace be upon him) himself — Ghazwa Al-Abwa' (Waddan) — with 70 men, in which he contracted a non-aggression pact with Bani Damrah; it took fifteen days, with a white flag carried by Hamzah.

In Rabi' Al-Awwal 2 A.H. came Buwat Invasion (200 companions, to intercept a caravan of 100 Quraishites and 2500 camels, Omaiya bin Khalaf among them) and Safwan Invasion (the preliminary Badr Invasion), when Karz bin Jabir raided the pastures of Madinah; the Prophet (Peace be upon him) pursued him to Safwan near Badr but could not catch him. In Jumada 2 A.H. came Dhil 'Ushairah Invasion (150-200 volunteers, to intercept the very Quraish caravan whose return from Syria would later cause the battle of Badr), during which he contracted a non-aggression pact with Bani Madlij and their allies Bani Dhumrah.

The Platoon of Nakhlah (Rajab 2 A.H.): the Messenger of Allah (Peace be upon him) despatched 'Abdullah bin Jahsh with 12 Emigrants, giving him a letter to be read only after two days, instructing him to go to Nakhlah (between Makkah and At-Ta'if) to watch a caravan and gather news. At Nakhlah a Quraish caravan passed; the Muslims debated fighting in Rajab, a sacred month, then engaged: 'Amr bin Al-Hadrami was killed, two were captured, and one escaped. They returned with booty and captives, but the Messenger disapproved and suspended action on account of the prohibited month. The polytheists exploited this to accuse the Muslims of violating the sacred month, until the Revelation gave a decisive answer: "They ask you concerning fighting in the sacred months. Say: Fighting therein is a great (transgression), but a greater transgression with Allah is to prevent mankind from following the way of Allah, to disbelieve in Him, to prevent access to Al-Masjid-Al-Harâm, and to drive out its inhabitants; and Al-Fitnah is worse than killing." [2:217]

After these events, Quraish realized the real danger Madinah posed, as the Muslims could now control an area of 300 miles, yet they remained obstinate and precipitated the great battle of Badr. The Muslims, at the behest of their Lord, were then ordered to war in Sha'ban 2 A.H.: "And fight in the way of Allah those who fight you, but transgress not the limits... And Al-Fitnah is worse than killing... And fight them until there is no more Fitnah and worship is for Allah alone. But if they cease, let there be no transgression except against the wrong-doers." [2:190-193] Allah also taught them the rules of fighting [47:4-7] and dispraised the hypocrites who feared it [47:20].

Another event of great significance occurred in Sha'ban 2 A.H. (February 624): the Divine injunction that Al-Qiblah be changed from Jerusalem to the Sacred Mosque in Makkah. This was of great advantage at two levels: it brought about a social sifting that revealed the hypocrites and purged the ranks, and it gently pointed to a new role awaiting the Muslims — for it was not logical to leave their Qiblah at the mercy of non-Muslims, foreshadowing their return to Makkah. The Muslims thereupon intensified their activities and their readiness to encounter Allah's enemies in a decisive battle.

topics.topicSummary: To secure the Makkan trade routes and deter Quraish, the Prophet ﷺ launched a series of pre-Badr reconnaissance patrols and expeditions (Saif Al-Bahr, Batn Rabegh, Al-Kharrar, Al-Abwa', Buwat, Safwan, Dhil 'Ushairah) — accrediting the first Muslim flag and forging non-aggression pacts. The Nakhlah platoon, which killed 'Amr bin Al-Hadrami in the sacred month, drew controversy answered by [2:217]. Full fighting was then ordained in Sha'ban 2 A.H. [2:190-193], the same month the Qiblah was changed to the Ka'bah — sifting the hypocrites and foreshadowing the return to Makkah.
